title: Design exercise: RAG service (retrieval-augmented generation)
summary: Design an internal, permission-aware question-answering service with hybrid retrieval, citations and team evaluation. Size chunks and tokens, publish versioned indexes safely, and map the neutral design to AWS without treating freshness or model quality as a managed-service guarantee.

exercise.prompt: Design an internal question-answering service over a company's documents (wikis, tickets, PDFs). A user asks a question and gets an answer with citations to the documents it came from. Several teams will put their own document sets on it.

constraints.caption: Exercise assumptions and targets; not measured production values.
rows: Ingest documents from several sources with incremental updates; answer a question with citations; respect document permissions (a user only gets answers from documents they may read); teams can evaluate answer quality on their own question sets.
2 million documents, average 20 kB of text, growing 2 percent per month.
20,000 questions per day, peak 2 per second; 50 teams. Derive chunks, vector bytes and token volume from these assumptions.
First token of the answer within 2 s at p50 and 5 s at p95; retrieval under 300 ms at p95; new or changed documents searchable within 15 minutes; model spend bounded per team.
Training or fine-tuning models, agents that take actions, chat memory beyond one conversation.

Yes; deletion must remove chunks and embeddings within the same 15 minutes.

blocks.text: There is no shared answer-cache fork: permissioned answers are not cached in this design. Provider prefix caching is optional and model-specific; no cache savings are assumed in the cost estimate. Titan Text Embeddings V2 supplies the selected vector dimension; its Bedrock admission quota is requests per minute, so ingestion batches still need request-rate planning separately from token billing.

blocks.text: This application's permission check linearises at the successful source-authority response for explicit tenant, user, document and immutable version tuples. The authority must validate that those versions are permitted at that instant; an eventually refreshed ACL copy cannot do so and unknown access fails closed. Fetch only those exact versions, never substitute a newer active version; missing bytes require fresh retrieval and authorisation. Both reranker and generator may use the authorised version set for this request even if revocation or a new version commits afterward. New requests require new checks. This is permitted in-flight continuation, not atomic check-and-release across services.

reference_answer.title: The core flow, step by step

blocks.text: The neutral ingestion protocol stages a complete version, then changes only the authoritative pointer.

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 1
  participant C as Connector
  participant D as Documents
  participant W as Worker
  participant I as Indexes

blocks.title: Publication, deletion and reconciliation rules
items: Stage the entire new document version; workers may retry deterministic chunk ids without duplicating visible content.

Publish with a conditional version check after completeness validation. Retrieval selects active candidate versions; once authorised for a request, their immutable bytes remain pinned for its in-flight continuation.

A delete denies new authority checks immediately when committed at that authority, then removes derived entries within the freshness target. Earlier authorised requests may continue under the stated contract.
Reconciliation compares source versions, active pointers and derived chunk counts; repair missing work from durable intents, not from assumed queue history.

Authorise exact candidate version tuples at the current authority, then fetch only those immutable versions. The same request authorisation covers reranker and generator despite later revocation; retry retrieval and authorisation if bytes are missing.

Before emitting text, reject absent authorised context and require citation instructions. Stream text only as provisional. Validate cited ids against that context and require citations before final success; missing or invalid citations or detected unsupported claims reject the whole answer and end with abstention, not a citation-free success. The client marks prior text rejected, but cannot retract bytes already seen. Membership is not proof of faithfulness: undetected unsupported claims remain a quality risk measured by evaluation.

blocks.text: Treat retrieval quality as an engineering loop. The Azure guide separates chunking, enrichment, embedding, search configuration and evaluation. This design runs each team’s expected-source queries before changing a chunker, embedding model or reranker. A new embedding model creates a new index version, never a mixture of incompatible vector spaces.

No blanket claim that training is cheaper.
Model-only answer if provenance is unnecessary

blocks.caption: Failure modes.
rows: Only policy-approved model fallback before output; otherwise return authorised source links with an explicit degraded state.
Current source authorisation or synchronously maintained authority; unknown fails closed.
one model per index version; rebuild per collection; never mix
separate bulk lane from incremental lane; backpressure; freshness metric per collection
invalid or missing citations reject the whole answer and end with abstention; prior provisional text is marked rejected, not silently accepted; membership does not prove faithfulness
indexes rebuildable from the document store; replicas for the large ones

blocks.text: A new version never overwrites the old visible version until all derived rows are ready. Queue redelivery is expected; version fencing and completeness checks, not the queue, provide idempotent publication.

blocks.caption: Neutral cost sensitivity, not a vendor quote: assumed generation prices only.

blocks.text: Immutable serving segments and quantisation become candidates for the largest collections, as in the vector-search exercise. They are not a reason to delete the document store: versioned originals and current authorisation remain the authority. The AWS table prices a different concrete model and explicitly excludes unquantified work.

L1: The ingestion pipeline (chunk, embed, index) and the query pipeline (retrieve, prompt, generate) with citations.
A vector store, permission filtering somewhere, and a latency budget.
L2: Hybrid retrieval and reranking with the reason; filtering before the model sees text; per-collection indexes.
Incremental updates and deletions with reconciliation; an evaluation set per team.
Token cost arithmetic and prompt caching; streaming for first-token latency; the embedding-model-change backfill.
L3: The vector index as a rebuildable derived view; evaluation as a release gate across teams.
Provider abstraction and fallback; tenancy and cost attribution as the platform questions.

The service refuses final success without citations or over unauthorised collections. Streamed text is provisional and is marked rejected on failed evidence checks; membership cannot prove faithfulness. Explain when search without generation or a small static FAQ is better.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: the six clarifying questions, the non-goals, and the numbers aloud: 20 million chunks, 81.92 GB of raw vectors (roughly 80 GB), 120 million input tokens per day (all assumptions), 2 questions per second at peak, 15-minute freshness.
0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: Collection, Document, Chunk, Question, EvalSet; the streaming ask endpoint, the idempotent sync endpoint, the evaluation run.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the diagram: the two pipelines, one index per collection, the permission filter before the reranker, the gateway in front of the model, the question log that feeds evaluation.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: retrieval quality as an evaluation loop (contextual chunks, hybrid retrieval, rerank, per-team eval sets as a release gate, re-embedding as a backfill), then permissions and tenancy (version-bound authority checks and permitted in-flight continuation, per-collection indexes, deletion, per-team budgets and cost per answer).
0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x plan, and the L3 sentence: the index is a derived view; the design is really about the document store, the ACLs and the evaluation loop.
Context and scope: The document sources, the teams, the permission systems of record, and the model provider in use today.
Goals and non-goals: Cited answers, strict permissions, 15-minute freshness, bounded spend per team; no fine-tuning, no agents, no long-term memory.
Design: This answer fills it: both pipelines, the data model, the diagram and the query path.
Alternatives considered: Index layout, permission enforcement, vector store, with the trade-off table.
Cross-cutting concerns: Privacy of question logs, cost per team, rollout per collection, observability of retrieval recall and freshness.
Review questions the doc must answer: The permission filter's correctness under ACL change, and the re-embedding plan when the embedding model changes.

depth_notes.L1: An ingestion pipeline (chunk, embed, index) and a query path (retrieve, rerank, generate) with citations.

depth_notes.L3: A RAG platform for many teams (index ownership, access control at retrieval, evaluation gates in CI, cost per answer, provider abstraction).
